newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan regulators talk tough on offshore futures.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan regulators talk tough on offshore futures.

text.p: Taiwan regulators on Wednesday took a hard line on unauthorised offshore Taiwan stock-index futures being launched on Thursday in Singapore and Chicago, vowing to ferret out illegal trading by local investors.

Securities and Exchange Commission Vice-Chairman Hsu Yung-pang told reporters Taiwan had not legalised local trading of the contracts being launched by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) and Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX).
Hsu urged investors not to try to trade the contracts through what he called "illegal futures brokerages" -- a phrase meaning any Taiwan futures house.

Brokerages in Taiwan, which has a major stock market but no futures exchange, are allowed to trade a range of commodities futures on overseas markets but trading of the CME and SIMEX contracts as well as Taiwan stock options being launched by San Francisco's Pacific Stock Exchange remains forbidden.
"We will cooperate with the Investigation Bureau to investigate any illegal trading on the futures index," Hsu said after a meeting with finance ministry officials.
He said local law prohibited local brokerages from placing orders for Taiwan investors through overseas affiliates and promised that violators would face "harsh punishment".
He did not address the question of whether investors who placed overseas orders themselves by telephone or other "underground" methods would be considered lawbreakers.
Hsu said his agency would decide "as soon as possible" whether to legalise local access to the contracts.

Stalling for time to build its own futures infrastructure, the commission has stopped short of deeming the offshore rivals hostile but has withheld technical cooperation and threatened to cut off access to stock price data crucial to their indices.
Finance Minister Paul Chiu took a more conciliatory line on Tuesday, saying Taiwan regarded the offshore index contracts as positive and planned to monitor their performance and impact.

Pressure to end the ban was expected to surge on Thursday if the new contracts attract active interest, and especially if the lack of access inside Taiwan fuels capital outflows big enough to destabilise the currency, stock and capital markets.
Experts estimate Taiwan stock-index futures could fuel T$50 billion (US$1.8 billion) a month in first-year turnover.

Taiwan regulators have voiced suspicion about the offshore contracts, saying their relatively small lot size gave them the appearance of being more speculative than merely risk-hedging instruments aimed at individuals rather than institutions.
Taiwan's own exchange, which had planned a mid-1997 start, has been delayed to 1998 due to parliament's prolonged bickering over several drafts of an enabling Futures Trading Law.
Taiwan brokers said the futures being launched on Thursday would make the local stock market more volatile at the outset but in the longer term would become an important price factor.
Volumes on the SIMEX and CME contracts should be relatively low until Taiwan investors gain legal access, brokers said.
